prompt: What does the lesson say adapting a message for a non-technical reader actually is?

choices.text: Removing the hard ideas so that the reader can follow without effort
choices.why: That is the picture the lesson starts by rejecting; the reader does not need fewer ideas.

choices.text: Translating each technical term into an analogy
choices.why: Analogies help with one point at a time and break when pushed; they are not the method.

choices.text: Changing the unit, the length and the ask
choices.why: Right: to fit what that reader decides.

choices.text: Sending the same message with a glossary attached at the end
choices.why: The message is still at the writer's altitude, with the reader asked to do the work.

prompt: Match each audience to the unit the lesson says it works in.

pairs.right: orders, hours of service, their own staff's work

prompt: Lívia tells Renata she needs "six engineer-weeks in April". By the lesson, what is missing for Renata?

choices.text: A reassurance that the work is easy and will finish early
choices.why: A promise of ease is not information, and the lesson never asks for one.

choices.text: What it displaces on the roadmap
choices.why: Right: "the substitution flow moves from April to May" is the sentence she needs.

choices.text: The hourly cost of an engineer
choices.why: Money is Caio's unit; Renata's is what gets built when.

choices.text: The technical design, so she can check it
choices.why: Renata decides order, not design; the design is the team's document.

prompt: What failure is typical of messages to the engineering team, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Stating the cost in reais
choices.why: Not harmful, just not their unit; the lesson names a different failure.

choices.text: Being too formal with people who sit nearby
choices.why: Tone is not the failure the lesson names.

choices.text: Too much detail, since engineers want one line
choices.why: Engineers want the constraints and detail and will check them.

choices.text: Leaving out the reason, so the change is undone later
choices.why: Right: a team told "use the replica" with no why removes it the first time it is inconvenient.

prompt: In the four versions of the replica decision, what is identical across all of them?

choices.text: The order in which the information comes
choices.why: Each version starts where its reader decides.

choices.text: The level of technical detail, which is kept constant to be fair to all readers
choices.why: Detail changes most of all; the version to Tânia has none.

choices.text: Every number they give
choices.why: Right: 180 failures, six engineer-weeks, R$ 4,000 a month, April.

choices.text: The length, about sixty words each
choices.why: The figure shows 44 to 87 words in the English versions.

prompt: Why does the board version mention the 6 March outage but not the replica?
hint: What has the board already heard, and what will it decide?

choices.text: To hide the technical approach from the board
choices.why: Nothing is hidden; it is just not their decision.

choices.text: The outage was more expensive than the fix
choices.why: That may be true and is not why it is mentioned.

choices.text: Replicas are too complicated for non-engineers to understand
choices.why: The lesson rejects that idea: the reason is the decision, not the reader's capacity.

choices.text: They heard about the outage; nobody there decides about replicas
choices.why: Right: include what connects to what they know, leave out what they will never act on.

prompt: What does the message to Tânia about the 24 April switch-over contain? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Why a read replica was chosen
choices.why: Nothing she decides depends on it.

choices.text: Who to call if something looks wrong
choices.why: Yes: Lívia directly.

choices.text: The cause of the 6 March outage
choices.why: Not her concern, and not in the message.

choices.text: What she must do, which is nothing
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: When it happens
choices.why: Yes: 24 April, 23:00 to 23:30.

prompt: How many words is the English version written for the engineering team, by the figure?
By the lesson, on which rung of the ladder should a message start?

choices.text: Where the reader's decision lives
choices.why: Right: and go down one rung only to support a claim they might doubt.

choices.text: The bottom, then climb so the reasoning is complete
choices.why: That is the shape of the message the CEO stops reading.

choices.text: The top, since the business view is always the most important
choices.why: Right for the board and wrong for Bruna's team, who decide lower down.

choices.text: The writer's own rung, since that is where the expertise is
choices.why: That is the natural rung and almost never the reader's.

prompt: In Elizabeth Newton's 1990 study, how many of the 120 tapped songs did the listeners name?
What did the tappers in Newton's study fail to imagine?
hint: They could hear something the listeners could not.

choices.text: How fast the listeners would guess
choices.why: The prediction was about how many, not how fast.

choices.text: That tapping on a table makes little sound
choices.why: Volume was not the issue.

choices.text: Hearing only the knocking, without the melody
choices.why: Right: knowing the tune, they could not unknow it, which is the curse of knowledge.

choices.text: That the listeners had never heard the songs before the experiment
choices.why: The songs were well known; the gap was in the tapping.

prompt: Lívia explains the database as "a shop with one till". What risk does the lesson see in pushing the analogy further?

choices.text: Analogies are unprofessional in work writing
choices.why: The lesson uses one approvingly, for one point.

choices.text: The reader may not have been to a shop
choices.why: It was chosen because everybody has.

choices.text: "Open another till" suggests the larger server the proposal rejected
choices.why: Right: the reader reasons from the part where the analogy breaks.

choices.text: It makes the problem sound smaller than 180 failures a week
choices.why: The size is stated separately; the danger the lesson names is the wrong fix.

prompt: The only reliable cure for the curse of knowledge, by the lesson, is to ask somebody from the ___ to read the message.
An engineer writes to a client: "It will be fixed by Monday." Why does the lesson treat this sentence with care?
hint: How a client reads a sentence.

choices.text: Clients do not want to hear about fixes at all
choices.why: They do; they want what changes for them and what happens next.

choices.text: Monday is a bad day for releases
choices.why: The day is not the problem.

choices.text: It is too vague; it should give the hour of the fix as well
choices.why: More precision makes the same unkeepable promise sharper.

choices.text: It is a promise with a date, and nobody is sure of it
choices.why: Right: say what you will do by Monday, not what will be true by then.

prompt: The logistics engineer's draft to Tânia carried which risks? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The size of the delay
choices.why: The draft never gives it; Lívia's version adds it.

choices.text: A colleague named
choices.why: Yes: Paulo.

choices.text: A promise nobody can keep for certain
choices.why: Yes: "should be fine tomorrow".

choices.text: A guessed cause
choices.why: Yes: "I think because of the new replica config".

prompt: Lívia commits to sending Tânia "what we found, and what we are changing, by Thursday at 12:00". Why that commitment and not "it will not happen again"?
hint: Which of the two is in her control?

choices.text: "It will not happen again" sounds too informal for a client of that size
choices.why: The problem is not tone; it is a promise nobody can be sure of.

choices.text: Keeping it does not depend on what the investigation finds
choices.why: Right: a commitment to act by a time, not a guarantee of an outcome.

choices.text: To delay the conversation until Tânia has calmed down
choices.why: She also offers to call before 7:00 if tomorrow is affected; nothing is being delayed.

choices.text: Thursday is the contractual deadline for incident reports
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson mentions such a clause.

prompt: Which apology belongs in a message to a client, by the lesson?
hint: A fact and a courtesy, not a legal statement.

choices.text: "We are sorry the deliveries were late"
choices.why: Right: true, courteous, and it claims nothing about cause.

choices.text: "We are sorry, Paulo's job ran late and took the database down"
choices.why: An internal name and a guessed cause in one sentence.

choices.text: "We are sorry our negligence caused the delay"
choices.why: It admits something that has not been established.

choices.text: "Sorry, the same thing happened with another chain last month"
choices.why: Other clients never appear in a message to a client.

prompt: The board hears "a small risk"; the team hears "this could take checkout down on any Friday". What does the lesson predict?

choices.text: Someone sets them side by side, and the writer stops being believed
choices.why: Right: from that day nothing the writer says is taken at face value.

choices.text: The team will tone its own messages down to match
choices.why: The lesson's point is about the writer's credibility, not the team's tone.

choices.text: The board will approve the fix faster
choices.why: A small risk is a reason to approve it more slowly, if at all.

choices.text: Nothing, since each message suits its audience
choices.why: The unit may change; the facts may not.
